data.title: Samsung, SK Hynix stocks plunge sharply: why over $8 billion has not calmed markets
data.description:
Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix stocks extended their slide on Monday as investors cut exposure to artificial intelligence-linked stocks, even as South Korea prepared a 10.76 trillion won ($8.02 billion) market support fund.

Samsung fell 4.72% and SK Hynix lost 4.13% by 11:20 am in Seoul. The benchmark KOSPI dropped 4.33%, after sinking as much as 5.81% earlier in the session.

By around 1 pm, the KOSPI had trimmed its decline to 3.74%.

The selling is increasingly at odds with the chipmakers' order books. Both companies have described strong demand for advanced memory, but investors are questioning whether the AI spending boom can sustain those profits and valuations.

Samsung, SK Hynix stocks: A Wall Street chip rout spills into Seoul

Friday's US semiconductor rout set the tone. Nvidia plunged 14.01%, Micron Technology lost 13.89% and AMD sank 13.25%, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index tumbled 10.73%.

The concern reaches beyond market sentiment for Samsung and SK Hynix. Their high-bandwidth memory chips are essential for training and running advanced AI models, leaving the manufacturers exposed to any reconsideration of data-centre investment.

Fresh US restrictions on Chinese access to advanced computing have made the outlook harder to price. So have questions about the returns on the billions being spent by cloud companies.

Kiwoom Securities analyst Han Ji-young warned that doubts about future AI earnings could prolong the correction even after steep declines.

KOSPI index today: Foreign investors sell into strong memory demand

Over the week to 20 November, overseas investors sold a net 4.52 trillion won of Korean equities, according to Aju Press. Samsung accounted for 1.79 trillion won of that selling and SK Hynix for another 940.1 billion won.

Those flows make a difference because the two stocks carry enormous weight in local benchmarks. When international funds reduce their Korean exposure, both can fall regardless of recent operating performance.

The fundamentals are less clear-cut than the share-price collapse suggests.

SK Hynix says contracts with 14 major customers cover more than half of its planned production capacity in 2027 and 2028.

Samsung's high-bandwidth memory supply for next year is effectively sold out. KB Securities' Kim Dong-won sees memory demand broadening beyond Nvidia to makers of custom AI chips.

But contracts cannot entirely remove the risk of delayed orders or lower prices. Investors must decide whether today's scarcity will persist once new chip capacity comes online.

South Korea's 10.76 trillion won backstop has limits

Officials have readied a stabilisation fund worth 10.76 trillion won, but have announced neither a deployment date nor any actual share purchases.

Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il argues that long-term orders and rapidly declining memory inventories support continued growth in AI chips.

Authorities also plan tougher monitoring of illegal short selling rather than another sweeping ban.

The fund may ease panic by signalling a willingness to intervene, but cannot determine how much customers spend on memory next year.

Han identified a severe downside scenario of 4,200–4,300 for the KOSPI, while judging it less likely given oversold conditions and the possibility of official support.

data.title: Crude oil price analysis as Iran’s IRGC seeks to challenge the US blockade
data.description:
Crude oil prices remained under pressure on Monday as investors assessed the state of the ongoing US-Iran war. Brent, the global benchmark, was trading at $93, down sharply from last month's high of $117.34. Oil will likely remain volatile as traffic through the Strait of Hormuz declines and as Iran attempts to test the US blockade.

Iran is considering breaking the US blockade

President Donald Trump remains under substantial pressure to end the war he started in February. Most of this pressure is coming from Israel, which has continued pushing for a resumption of war. Benjamin Netanyahu and his team has shared intelligence warning that Iran was considering a dirty bomb. He has also warned that Iran was considering using chemical weapons. 

Many neocons, including Mark Levin, General Jack Keane, and Nikki Haley have also pushed Trump to “finish the job.” By finishing the job, they have urged him to arm the “opposition” and attack Kharg Island and other energy infrastructure. 

Trump, on the other hand, has been cautious for several reasons. For one, he knows that Iran will retaliate by launching attacks against Gulf allies. Iran has also warned that it will attack data centers, desalination plants, airports, and even cut the internet cables that pass through the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump also knows that Iran will not capitulate and that the US is running dangerously low on ammunition. As a result, there is fear that he will maintain the status quo of the blockade and sanctions. 

Now, however, there are signs that Iran is plotting to challenge the blockade by sending at least 14 tankers through the Strait. The IRGC has warned that it will launch major attacks against Gulf energy infrastructure if the US attacks any of these ships. If Iran is able to break the blockade, then oil flows from the region will start rising.

Iran has intensified tanker attacks

A major risk facing the energy market is that Iran has continued launching attacks against ships crossing through the Strait. The IRGC has attacked tens of tankers, while several others have hit sea mines. As a result, the cost of crossing through the Strait has soared, with insurance jumping from $56,000 before the war to over $60 million today. 

Recent data shows that the number of ships crossing through the Strait has dropped substantially in the past few weeks. This trend will likely continue as Iran’s attacks accelerate and as the deal between the two sides remains elusive. 

Crude oil price technical analysis

Brent crude oil price chart | Source: TradingView

The daily chart shows that Brent has been in a strong sell-off in the past few weeks. It has now slumped from a high of $117.3 to the current $93. There are signs that oil is losing the downward momentum along the 200-day Exponential Moving Average (EMA). 

It has also formed a small double-bottom pattern, which is a common bullish reversal sign in technical analysis. Therefore, there is a likelihood that Brent will bounce back, potentially to the psychological level of $100. A drop below the support level of $89.23 will invalidate the bullish outlook.

data.title: Why is South Korea's KOSPI crashing despite a government rescue pledge?
data.description:
South Korean stocks tumbled on Monday as renewed selling in semiconductor shares overwhelmed government assurances that emergency support would be available if market conditions deteriorated further.

The KOSPI fell as much as 5.8% to 4,586.80 in intraday trading, following Friday's 5.21% loss that left the benchmark at a 10-month closing low.

Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il said authorities were preparing to intervene if necessary, but stopped short of announcing purchases through the country's market-stabilization fund.

The rout underscores how concerns about AI valuations and tighter US technology restrictions are overshadowing expectations of solid Korean economic growth.

Samsung, SK Hynix stocks bear the brunt of AI selling

Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix led Monday’s chip stock sell-off, falling about 5.5% and 4.9%. Their heavy weighting in the benchmark makes declines particularly damaging to the wider market.

Investors are increasingly questioning whether the vast spending planned for AI data centres can sustain the earnings growth built into technology valuations. Tighter US rules governing access to advanced computing have added uncertainty for Asian suppliers.

The pressure has also been compounded by overseas selling. LSEG figures cited in recent market reporting show foreign investors heading for a seventh consecutive month of net Korean equity sales, with cumulative outflows of $115.2 billion.

Kiwoom Securities analyst Han Jiyoung has warned that the market needs a catalyst to bring foreign investors back despite strong corporate earnings.

KOSPI index today: Seoul readies a safety net without deploying it

Following an emergency meeting on Sunday, the government said it would complete preparations to activate its securities market stabilisation fund when conditions warranted.

Lee told reporters in Sejong on Monday that officials had additional contingency measures and would act according to market conditions.

Authorities also plan to relax daily limits on listed companies' share buyback orders for three months from Tuesday, giving businesses greater flexibility to support their own shares.

Financial regulators will intensify monitoring of illegal short selling and market manipulation over the same period.

But Lee rejected calls for sweeping new short-selling restrictions, favouring stronger enforcement of existing rules. South Korea lifted its previous blanket ban in March 2025 after establishing a centralised detection system.

The distinction matters, as preparing financial firepower may reassure investors, but it is not the same as injecting capital into the market.

KOSPI crash: Strong economic forecasts clash with falling share prices

Lee still expects economic momentum to remain robust. He said growth could reach the upper-3% range in 2026 if current trends persist, and projected continued expansion next year.

The International Monetary Fund recently forecast growth of 3.9% this year and 3.3% in 2027, supported by semiconductor exports and investment.

However, for investors, near-term risk is taking precedence over those projections. Lee warned that volatility in AI-related industries could spill into the wider economy, while geopolitical uncertainty and higher global interest rates remained threats.

The next test is whether the government's preparations can arrest selling without an actual fund deployment, or whether another decline forces Seoul to move beyond reassurance.

data.title: Crypto Fear and Greed Index slumps to 7: Can Bitcoin, Ethereum and XRP rebound?
data.description:
The Crypto Fear and Greed Index has been in a strong sell-off this month as Bitcoin and most altcoins have continued their plunge. It dropped to the extreme fear zone of 7, down sharply from the year-to-date high of over 72. 

Bitcoin has slumped to $60,000 from the October high of $87,586. Ethereum has plunged to $1,662, down by over 40% from its highest point in September. XRP has also fallen by over 60% from its peak in September.

Crypto Fear and Greed Index has plunged

There is a sense in which fear is spreading in the market. The Crypto Fear and Greed Index has tumbled to 7. This is important because the index is created by looking at several major data points, including price momentum, volatility, derivative markets, market composition, and proprietary data. 

The same trend is happening with the CNN Money Fear and Greed Index, which has dropped to the extremely fear zone of 10. Most of its gauges, including market momentum, stock price breadth, put and call options, market volatility, safe-haven demand, and junk bond demand have tumbled to the extreme fear zone. 

These metrics have moved amid major risks in the market. For example, there are signs that the artificial intelligence (AI) bubble is about to burst, which explains why most companies in the industry have plunged. This includes popular names like SanDisk, Marvell Technologies, and Nvidia.

At the same time, there are signs that the Federal Reserve will hike interest rates in the next meeting. Recent data showed that the economy created over 165k jobs last month, while the unemployment rate fell to 4.2%.

Binance hack and ETF outflows

Meanwhile, the Crypto Fear and Greed Index dropped because of the recent Binance hackthat cost the company billions of dollars. North Korean hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance. Binance talked to Circle and Tether, which managed to freeze about $3 billion of these funds. The company has also used its funds to top up the funds. 

Some analysts believe that the Binance hack marked a turning point in the ongoing crypto winter. For one, if Binance, the biggest crypto exchange can be hacked, then no other company is safe. 

Meanwhile, investors have continued selling their crypto ETFs. Bitcoin ETFs have suffered over $3.5 billion in outflows this month after they shed $550 million last month. Ethereum and XRP ETFs have also shed substantial assets in the past few weeks. In most cases, these outflows tend to signal that investors are starting to capitulate. 

The same trend is happening in the futures market, where open interest has been in a strong sell-off. Falling open interest is a sign that leveraged investors are not buying the coin. One reason for this is that Democrats have retaken the House of Representatives and Senate, opening the door for more regulations.

Technicals also signaling that cryptocurrencies have more downside to go. Bitcoin and Ethereum have all formed a death cross pattern, pointing to a sustained sell-off. These technicals mean that Bitcoin and altcoins may fall further.

On the positive side, US bond yields are falling, which is a positive thing for risky asssets. The drop has coincided with the falling US stock market. As such, with equities plunging, there are signs that the Fed will not hike rates aggressively. In fact, the CME Fed Futures tool shows that the probability is that the bank will hike by 0.25%. Just last week, there was expectation that the Fed would hike by 0.50%.

data.title: Will Jensen Huang’s ouster push founders to secure more voting rights?
data.description:
Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia has raised questions for investors regarding how much power a star founder has over their company.

Despite having a substantial stake in his company, Huang didn’t have special voting rights in Nvidia, which reduced his autonomy during a crisis. 

This is in contrast to companies like SpaceX, Meta, and Anthropic, where founders have more voice in controlling the company due to special voting shares. 

Would Huang still be CEO if he had special voting rights? And would his exit prompt more founders to give them more voting power in their companies?

Huang’s ownership in Nvidia

Jensen Huang is the largest individual shareholder of the company. 

The former CEO who founded the company owned around 3.58% of the company's shares until March 2026, according to the company’s 2026 proxy statement. 

That amounted to around 870.6 million shares, much higher than current interim CEO Colette Kress’s 4.4 million shares. 

However, Nvidia’s voting structure consists of a single share giving a single vote, which means Huang couldn’t override a decision that would be made by the board. 

Huang also didn’t have special voting rights or privileges that sometimes other companies provide for their CEO.

So when push came to shove, Huang was a lame duck. 

Nvidia, in its latest results, also said that it wasn’t planning to bring Huang back despite him indicating he is ready to return to the company.

Other companies having special voting rights

There are numerous instances of companies providing CEOs or founders of their companies special voting rights to protect the CEO’s vision for the company.

Elon Musk owns around 48% of shares in SpaceX, where he has 6.4 billion shares, according to an SEC filing in August. 

These shares include Class A and Class B common stock, with Class A having one vote per share and Class B stock providing 10 votes per share. 

Musk owns around 3.9 billion Class B shares. This, combined with Class A shares, gives him 80% voting rights in the company. 

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg also has dual class structure shares within his Meta shares. 

The company’s 2026 proxy statement in March showed that Zuckerberg owned 342.5 million shares, which makes up around 13% of the shares in the company.

However, 341.82 million shares among these are Class B shares. Zuckerberg owns 99.8% of Class B shares, which gives him 60% of the voting power in the company. 

Anthropic, which is set to debut this week, also has a special ownership structure. 

The seven founders in the company, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and President Daniela Amodei, will be members of an entity called Founder LLC, which will have 50.1% of the total voting rights in the company. 

This structure would provide the board with unusual powers and limit the influence of institutional and retail investors.

“Our governance structure is likely to have the effect of limiting the likelihood of an unsolicited merger proposal, unsolicited tender offer, or proxy contest for the removal of directors. As a result, our governance structure may make it more difficult to replace our directors and management and may have the effect of depriving our stockholders of an opportunity to sell their shares at a premium over prevailing market prices”, the company said in its prospectus. 

Huang’s ouster could prompt more founders to give themselves voting rights to protect themselves from the board’s actions. 

Anna Wu, Founder of Floodlines Research, told Invezz that “Founders could well take Nvidia's experience as a reason to ask for super-voting shares.”

However, she added that the situation is different for US tech companies, as the situation could become a national security affair, as it happened with Nvidia.

“I wouldn't be surprised to see the government step in, and investors asking for curbs to avoid situations like this. We may end up seeing super-voting shares with carve-outs: matters, such as misconduct or national security, where founders' extra votes don't apply”, the expert added.

Would a dual-class structure have protected Huang?

Analysts said that Huang might not have defended himself even with a dual-class voting structure, as the issue pertained more to whether Huang shared company secrets with an alleged foreign spy.

Michael Hewson of MCH Market Insights told Invezz, “I think having dual-class structures would have helped, in terms of him being able to push back on his departure; however, it doesn’t change the narrative around the underlying issues along with his judgement. That, for me, is the story, along with his credibility.”

He added that while Musk and Zuckerberg are many things, they haven’t been caught up with “concerns over possible espionage.”

Anna Wu also said voting structure wouldn’t have protected Huang. 

“What made Huang's position untenable wasn't just a personal scandal; it was a potential national-security affair. Once Washington is involved, super-voting shares can't protect a CEO. Regulators, Congress and customers carry weight that shareholder votes don't”, she added.

Can Jensen come back to Nvidia?

In the company’s latest earnings call, Nvidia’s new board chairman, Harvey Jones, said that the company didn’t intend to bring Huang back.

The chairman also didn’t take questions regarding the resignation. 

Nvidia’s results, which surpassed market expectations, would have closed the door for Huang to come back for now. 

Analysts said that the return of the charismatic CEO would depend on the results of the investigation. 

“As for Huang coming back to Nvidia, anything is possible, especially if it’s proven that there are questions about the espionage angle. In this case, the passing of time may well offer Huang a route back, especially if Nvidia were to struggle without him,” Hewson said. 

“If the investigation clears him on the national-security question, a return can't be ruled out, because no one knows Nvidia better. If it doesn't, the door is effectively closed.” Wu noted.

The Jensen Huang episode shows that investors should also consider the personal behaviour of talismanic CEOs, as it could lead to national security complications. 

Anna Wu said, “Personally, I like a co-CEO set-up, or any structure that gives enough risk oversight. AI has lowered the information barrier, so any scandal now spreads quickly and widely. The best plan is simple: even rockstar founders need checks around them.”

Jensen Huang's case is unique, and experts agree that having special voting rights would not have protected him during the crisis.

More founders might provide themselves with voting rights, as in the case of Anthropic and SpaceX, to ensure they have power over the company's boards and shareholders to execute their vision.

However, Special voting rights cannot protect a founder when national security or regulatory concerns emerge.

The post Will Jensen Huang’s ouster push founders to secure more voting rights? appeared first on Invezz

data.title: Russian exchanges cleared to trade crypto as Bank of Russia rules take effect
data.description:
Russian exchanges can now launch organised trading in cryptocurrencies, after a Bank of Russia instruction setting out the rules for the market came into force on November 22, 2026.

There is a catch: each exchange first needs the central bank to agree its trading rules. No exchange had started trading by Sunday, and the first pilot deals are not expected until December.

What the Bank of Russia requires

The central bank announced the ordinance on 11 November, after Russia's Ministry of Justice registered it. Exchanges may begin crypto trading from 22 November "provided that they obtain the regulator's concurrence with their trading rules", it said.

Exchanges must register trading participants such as brokers, trust managers and central counterparties. They must also keep registers of orders and transactions and monitor trading.

They will have to calculate current, weighted average, market and closing prices, and report on trading to the Bank of Russia in the same way as for other assets.

State news agency TASS confirmed on Sunday that the instruction had taken effect, adding that earlier reports expected actual trading to begin after 1 December.

Retail access is capped

A separate ordinance, in force since 17 November, sets the terms for ordinary investors. Non-qualified investors can buy only bitcoin, ether and the USDT stablecoin.

They can buy through brokers, trust managers or crypto exchange offices, on exchange or over the counter. Purchases through any single intermediary are capped at ₽300,000 a year.

Every investor, qualified or not, must pass a test and read about the risks before trading. Qualified investors have access to all cryptoassets without restriction, the Bank of Russia said.

Moscow Exchange targets 1 December

Moscow Exchange said on 2 November that it plans to let market participants trade digital currencies from 1 December, creating what it called Russia's first organised digital currency market.

The first stage will involve pilot trades, with participants connected gradually as they become ready. The launch list covers BTC, ETH and USDT, with same-day (TOD) and next-day (TOM) settlement and swaps for liquidity management.

Trades will be cleared through the group's National Clearing Centre, and trading hours will match the stock market, from 06:50 to 23:50 Moscow time, the exchange said.

A notice on the Bank of Russia's website shows it registered new Moscow Exchange admission rules on 17 November, including a section for the digital currency market.

SPB Exchange still waiting

Rival SPB Exchange is further behind. Chief executive Evgeny Serdyukov said on 18 November that it had sent its trading and clearing rules to the central bank and was awaiting registration, Interfax reported.

"The Bank of Russia officially allows it on the 22nd, but for us to start trading, our documents also need to be registered," he said (Invezz translation). The exchange also needs a settlement digital depositary licence.

Serdyukov said he expected only isolated crypto deals this year, with market participants offering the service at scale only next year.

Onshoring, under sanctions

The framework is designed to pull crypto trading that Russians now do on offshore platforms onto supervised domestic venues. Invezz reported in February that Russia was considering blocking foreign crypto exchanges once the new regime was in place.

Foreign participation is likely to be limited. Moscow Exchange and its National Clearing Centre have been under US sanctions since June 2024, CoinDesk reported.

CoinDesk also noted that USDT issuer Tether freezes wallets on the US sanctions list, raising questions over how the stablecoin will be handled through the clearing house.

What happens next

The date to watch is 1 December, when Moscow Exchange plans its first pilot trades. SPB Exchange needs both its rules registered and a depositary licence before it can open.

For retail traders, the Russian model adds a mandatory test and an annual cap to the steps covered in Invezz's guide on how to buy bitcoin. Readers comparing venues elsewhere can see our ranking of the best crypto exchanges.

data.title: FT finds Alice Huang linked to chip network with alleged Cambodian crime group
data.description:
A Financial Times investigation has found that Alice Huang, the businesswoman romantically linked to former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, was connected to a network that supplied AI chips to China-based users. The FT says it included an alleged Cambodian criminal enterprise.

The FT says the web also took in Nvidia's cloud partners, gaming entrepreneurs and hundreds of shell companies. Together they made billions of dollars from moving restricted chips into China, the paper says, without necessarily knowing the full picture.

Alice Huang is at the centre of US inquiries into whether Megaspeed, Nvidia's largest client in south-east Asia, took part in the underground chip trade. Some US officials suspect she was a Chinese spy; Beijing calls that a "smear". No charges against her have been reported.

What the investigation found

The FT spoke to over a dozen people and traced links through hundreds of corporate filings. Diverting chips, it says, takes three things: a group allowed to buy and resell them, customers that pass US checks, and an underground route for hardware and money.

The first piece, it says, was Inspur, a major Nvidia partner for building chip servers in China. Washington put Inspur on its entity list in March 2023 over alleged help for the Chinese military. Its part-owned San Jose unit was not listed.

That unit was renamed Aivres and kept trading with Nvidia. A person with direct knowledge told the FT that staff inside Nvidia questioned whether Aivres should qualify as a partner. Nvidia decided it met all compliance and export-control rules.

The second piece was a buyer able to clear Nvidia's checks, which include three years of records and proof of non-Chinese ownership. Some Inspur clients sought help from Century Huatong, a Chinese gaming group that had become a data-centre investor.

The answer, according to the FT's sources, was an offshore shell branded a "neocloud" provider. That shell became Megaspeed. Alice Huang was its "trusted" outward-facing executive, they said.

What the people involved say

Nvidia says its shipments were all legal and authorised by the US government, spokesman John Rizzo said this week, according to The Business Times. Nvidia said in June 2025 it placed Megaspeed on its block list.

Megaspeed says it operates "fully within the bounds" of export controls, CNBC reported, and that Alice Huang left in August 2025. Reuters has not been able to reach her.

Invezz found no public response from Century Huatong or Aivres to the FT's findings.

China's foreign ministry calls the spy claim "unsubstantiated" and "nothing but smears", the Associated Press reported. Attorney General Todd Blanche said on 12 November the Justice Department had reached no conclusion on whether she was a spy.

How we got here

It began on 29 October, when the New York Times reported that US intelligence suspected Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive, of being a Chinese asset. Nvidia said Jensen Huang's contacts with her were ordinary customer meetings.

On 8 November, Nvidia's board opened an independent investigation into whether Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Huang admitted he had been unfaithful to his wife, without naming the woman.

The board accepted his resignation as CEO, president and director on 11 November, according to Nvidia's SEC filing, and announced it the next day. Chief financial officer Colette Kress became interim CEO.

On 12 November, Singapore said police had investigated Alice Huang over Megaspeed's server purchases and found insufficient evidence of an offence. She got a stern warning for giving inaccurate information and was barred from returning. The probe did not concern espionage, it said.

On 17 November, the Commerce and Justice departments said they had been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 and had interviewed Alice Huang in June 2025. Jensen Huang has agreed to a transcribed interview with three House committees on 1 December.

On 19 November, House Democrats asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick whether Nvidia influenced that investigation, Reuters reported. Nvidia said it looks forward to engaging with Congress.

What it means for Nvidia shares

Nvidia closed on Friday at $125.53, down 14% on the day. That is about 28% below its 11 November close of $173.73, the last before the resignation was announced (Invezz calculation).

The drop followed a Reuters report that SEC staff are examining potential accounting issues at Nvidia. Reuters noted that investigations are not evidence of wrongdoing.

It was Nvidia's seventh straight weekly fall, the longest run since 2008. The slide began before the scandal, amid worries over AI spending and rival chips.

data.title: Is Nvidia's Colette Kress standing on a glass cliff?
data.description:
A founder-CEO of an all-important global AI company, with a rockstar persona, admits to an affair with an alleged spy.

He is made to resign with the whole world watching and many powerful people rooting for his return, while waxing eloquent about why he is indispensable and irreplaceable.

A significant section of employees, at least a fourth of the workforce, feel wronged on his behalf, showing where their loyalties lie.

Many Shareholders want him back while the stock is in steady decline

It is in these evidently hostile conditions that a senior woman executive has been brought in to steady the ship while the company looks for a permanent successor.

Nvidia CFO Colette Kress’s appointment as interim chief of a company seen as the linchpin of the global AI boom is among the toughest jobs in the world right now.

It has also reignited the debate around the glass cliff phenomenon.

What is the glass cliff?

The term describes the widespread practice of preferentially appointing women or other minority employees to leadership positions in times of crisis, when the chances of failure are highest.

That makes it even harder for them to perform, eventually reinforcing the perception that women cannot lead.

It was coined by British academics Michelle Ryan and Alex Haslam, who in 2004 published an extensive study of FTSE 100 companies and found that women tended to be appointed to lead failing organisations.

A pattern that runs through history

Examples abound.

Marissa Mayer became Yahoo’s CEO in 2012, when the internet major had lost substantial market share and was struggling with focus and innovation.

She was its fifth CEO in five years, a sign of how volatile the company was.

Ellen Pao at Reddit, Roz Brewer at Walgreens Boots, even Theresa May becoming UK prime minister right after Brexit: all are telltale signs of the insidious phenomenon.

In a study conducted by Alison Cook, professor of management at the Jon M Huntsman School of Business at Utah State University, and her colleague Christy Glass, professor at the university’s school of social sciences, the researchers found that in US college men’s basketball, coaches from racial minorities were more likely than white coaches to be promoted to losing teams.

In 2013, the duo analysed CEO transitions in Fortune 500 companies over 15 years.

They found that occupational minorities, defined as white women and men and women of colour, were more likely than white men to be promoted CEO of weakly performing firms.

They also found that when performance declined under occupational minority CEOs, these leaders were likely to be replaced by white men, a pattern they termed the “savior effect.”

Does Nvidia fit the picture?

Invezz asked Cook whether Kress’s appointment amounts to a glass cliff, given that Nvidia is doing exceptionally well financially and has strong prospects.

“The glass cliff isn’t only about weak performance. It’s about being appointed to a precarious situation,” Cook told Invezz.

“In my work with Dr. Christy Glass, we’ve treated firms facing a scandal, including the firing of the previous CEO, or going through major restructuring as glass cliff situations too. Nvidia fits that picture. Kress is stepping in during a national security investigation, several lawsuits, and a permanent CEO search that may not pick her,” she said.

Cook spells out the challenges Kress faces and the conditions she is leading under, which make this a compelling case of the phenomenon.

“First, the scrutiny will be enormous. Nvidia is one of the most visible companies in the world, and every decision she makes will be watched and second-guessed. Second, her authority may be challenged. She is leading while there is a very public push to bring her predecessor back, which can make it hard for anyone to lead with full support. Third, the reputational risk falls on her."

"She is now the face of the company during a crisis she didn’t create, and if things go badly, she may be the one who wears it. So while the business itself is strong, the circumstances around her appointment fit the glass cliff mould,” she said.

Why organisations turn to women in a crisis

Sophie Williams, former global manager of production planning at Netflix, and author of The Glass Cliff: Why Women in Power Are Undermined – And How to Fight Back, has explained why organisations turn to women in moments of crisis.

“There’s a perception that when a team has gone through a hard time, what we are looking for suddenly becomes someone to make us feel better. Someone to play office mum, someone to soothe those experiences and those team members. And not necessarily make transformational change, as they say, but to just make people feel better in that experience,” she said in an earlier interview with Harvard Business Review.

“But because we are not bringing these women in with expectation of transformational changemaking, even when they are capable of it, it means that we don’t often give them either the tools or the time that are necessary to turn that perceived failure into a success before they’re exited. And so we see female leaders being 24% more likely to be fired than their male counterparts. We also see them having significantly shorter tenures in role once they are there,” she said.

The “office adult” label

Bloomberg columnist Beth Kowitt makes a similar point: “If the default for men in tech is charismatic genius, for senior women it is still way too often the office adult.”

Kowitt notes that Sheryl Sandberg, as chief operating officer at Meta Platforms Inc., played the “polished grownup” to counterbalance Mark Zuckerberg’s “hoodie-wearing, college-dropout persona.”

Linda Yaccarino, as CEO of X, had to “clean up the mess left in the wake of Elon Musk.”

The label, she says, implies “a certain kind of executive; one who ensures everyone is well-behaved and on schedule, who brings stability and credibility — but not necessarily big vision.”

“For a generation of women, that may have been the only way in the door,” she says, drawing a comparison with Kress.

Reports that Huang called Kress a “deer in the headlights”, a 'reporting CEO' who could not help him set strategy, have already set a lens through which to view her: as a second fiddle, not thought of much by the rockstar founder-CEO.

To be sure, as Kowitt points out, Kress was hired after Huang interviewed 22 candidates, and said he wanted her to be CFO "for as long as we shall live.”

Kress to run two of the company’s most important jobs

Those who see Kress’s appointment as a glass cliff also point out that she must now run the two most important functions at the company, a daunting task despite Kress' credentials and expertise.

Nvidia is the unofficial financier of the AI boom, spreading its vast cash piles as investments in budding AI startups, including OpenAI and Anthropic, and in ecosystem players such as neoclouds like CoreWeave.

Her role as CFO is therefore far from that of a mere bean counter.

Kress is a seasoned executive. She has spent 13 years at Nvidia, after nearly 25 years in finance roles at major technology companies such as Cisco, Microsoft and Texas Instruments.

Even so, does holding both jobs set her up to fail?

“I wouldn’t call holding both roles a set-up on its own. Interim CEOs who keep their CFO role aren’t unheard of,” Cook said.

She pointed to HP, which in 2010 named Cathie Lesjak interim CEO in addition to her CFO role after Mark Hurd left.

Lesjak served about three months before the board went outside for its next CEO.

“What concerns me more is authority and support. My work with Dr. Christy Glass found that women CEOs often lack the support or authority to accomplish their strategic goals,” she said.

More recently, Cook said, her research with Glass and Dr Alicia Ingersoll found that women CEOs have shorter tenures than men and are more likely to be dismissed involuntarily.

The gap widens when women are appointed during weak organisational performance.

Authority, loyalty and credit

On the earnings call this week, the board ruled out bringing Huang back, after a massive campaign for his reinstatement backed by shareholders, former and current employees, and supporters including Elon Musk and US President Donald Trump.

But the decision alone will not quickly change sentiment.

Cook also points out that Huang’s family remains inside the company.

His daughter, Madison Huang, holds a senior role, and his son and son-in-law are in leadership positions too.

“If coalitions form around his return, or people simply fail to support her, she is leading without full authority,” she said.

Finally, Cook turns to the financing question.

“Sources describe Kress as potentially more conservative than Huang, and she has sometimes pushed back on deals he championed. If she pulls back and growth slows, she may get the blame. If things go well, the credit may go to the foundation Jensen built."

"In other words, she may get the blame if things go wrong but not the credit if they go right. As one executive in our research put it, ‘If you don’t produce magic in a short period of time, then they say this isn’t working.’”

A baptism by fire

Earlier this week, Kress faced her first earnings call as interim chief rather than just as CFO.

Observers scrutinised not only what she said but also her tone of voice, an early example of the pressure she will face.

Many experts made note that she relied heavily on scripted remarks and sounded robotic and monotone, while some also wrote about her nervousness.

The sceptics

There are, of course, those who reject both the view that Kress’s appointment is a glass cliff and the phenomenon itself.

Last month, a senior McKinsey partner was removed from his leadership roles after LinkedIn posts questioning the phenomenon drew criticism.

Chris Bradley, who is based in Australia, was until recently one of a handful of directors at the McKinsey Global Institute, the consulting firm’s business and economics research arm.

He questioned whether the phenomenon existed at all.

In the now-deleted posts, he called the glass cliff “a very convenient way to always be a victim in the rain.”

On Nvidia specifically, a recent LinkedIn thread on the phenomenon drew a comment from Stan Clark, advisor at Infocrest Solutions and a former senior director at Oracle.

“Colette Kress has earned this. Thirteen years as Nvidia’s CFO, through the company’s biggest growth years. She knows the customers, the numbers, and the team,” Clark said.

“Safra Catz showed what a leader with that background can do. She took on the co-CEO role at Oracle, then led the company after Mark Hurd passed away, and she was exceptional. My bet is on Colette. Rooting for her and the whole Nvidia team.”

The CFO-to-CEO trend

Cook says her findings show that glass cliff appointments are often the culmination of a long-term, risk-centred career strategy.

“Because these leaders are highly visible as outsiders but often invisible as leaders, many deliberately take on risky, high-profile assignments throughout their careers to prove their mettle. That pays off, but it comes with what we call a risk tax: a standard of perfection where one mistake can end a career, constant fear of derailment, and real performance fatigue over time,” she says.

The growing trend of CFOs becoming CEOs may also be cited to question whether Kress’s appointment is a glass cliff.

In 2025, 10.26% of sitting CEOs at Fortune 500 and S&P 500 firms came directly from the CFO role, the highest share in a decade, according to Crist Kolder Associates’ 2025 Volatility report, released on Jan. 28.

In 2024, the figure was 7.1%.

Recent corporate moves bear this out.

Toyota this year appointed CFO Kenta Kon as president and CEO, succeeding Koji Sato.

Unilever named CFO Fernando Fernandez as CEO, succeeding Hein Schumacher.

“The CFO-to-CEO trend is real. CFO-to-CEO promotions are at a decade high, and those promotions have been internal. So on its face, an internal CFO stepping up fits current practice,” Cook says.

“My sense, though, is that tech firms, and chip companies especially, lean toward leaders with engineering and product backgrounds, so I’m less sure the CFO trend holds as strongly there.”

What happens next

Cook, however, urges a focus on what comes next.

“The bigger point is that you can’t separate the two by looking at the appointment alone. You have to look at what happens next. Is she seriously considered for the permanent role? Is she given the authority and support to actually lead? And if she is replaced, by whom and why?" she says.

"In my work with Dr. Christy Glass, we found that when firm performance declined under women and minority CEOs, they were likely to be replaced by white men, which we call the savior effect. These leaders are given fewer degrees of freedom to lead their firms out of crisis. Lesjak served as a bridge at HP and went back to the CFO role when the board brought in an outsider. Whether Kress follows that path or is genuinely in the running will tell us a lot.”

Meanwhile, Nvidia’s recruitment firm has reportedly approached Rene Haas, CEO of Arm, in its search for a new chief executive.

Haas spent seven years at Nvidia before joining Arm in 2013. He became Arm’s CEO in 2022 and has since overseen its expansion into the booming AI infrastructure market.

data.title: Michael Burry takes profits on Nvidia puts as chip stocks extend sell-off
data.description:
Michael Burry, the investor made famous by The Big Short, has taken profits on part of his bearish bets against Nvidia and the semiconductor sector following a sharp technology sell-off this week.

In a Friday update to subscribers of his Cassandra Unchained Substack, Burry said he sold 50% of his put options on Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) and the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH), locking in what he described as substantial gains.

He retained the remaining half of both positions.

Put options increase in value when the underlying shares decline, allowing investors to profit from falling stock prices.

Burry also reduced some of his bullish exposure, selling roughly one-third of his call options on animal health company Zoetis (NYSE: ZTS) to secure gains.

However, he left his bearish April 2027 put options on the Nasdaq 100 untouched, maintaining his longer-term negative outlook on large-cap technology stocks.

Burry increases MercadoLibre stake

Alongside the profit-taking, Burry increased his position in Latin American e-commerce company MercadoLibre (NASDAQ: MELI) by 20%.

He also pointed to what he described as "absolute relative strength" in several stocks, including healthcare companies Molina Healthcare (NYSE: MOH) and HCA Healthcare (NYSE: HCA), software company Adobe (NASDAQ: ADBE) and grocery retailer Sprouts Farmers Market (NASDAQ: SFM).

The portfolio changes indicate that Burry is adjusting some of his positions following the recent market moves while retaining his bearish exposure to the Nasdaq 100.

His decision to lock in part of his Nvidia and semiconductor ETF gains came as chip stocks endured a difficult week, with Nvidia extending its losing streak despite reporting strong quarterly results.

Nvidia shares extend losing streak

Nvidia shares fell for a seventh consecutive session on Friday and were on track for their worst weekly performance since November 2018.

The decline came despite the chipmaker reporting record quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion, more than double the year-earlier figure.

Net profit increased 109% to $64.9 billion, beating Wall Street forecasts.

Interim CEO Colette Kress also provided a strong outlook, forecasting fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion and raising the company's fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook to 75%.

However, the earnings performance did little to support the stock as investors continued to assess concerns surrounding the company and the broader technology sector.

Nvidia has also faced scrutiny over allegations involving the potential diversion of advanced chips to China.

Two House Democrats reportedly opened an inquiry into whether the company sought to influence the Commerce Department's investigation of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud company suspected of illegally diverting advanced chips to China.

Separately, Representative Brett Guthrie, chairman of the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, sent a letter to Kress requesting that Nvidia officials appear before the panel by December 2.

Semiconductor sell-off weighs on technology stocks

Nvidia's decline spread across the wider semiconductor sector, adding to pressure on technology stocks as investors questioned whether substantial spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure would generate sufficient returns.

The Invesco QQQ ETF (QQQ), which tracks the Nasdaq 100, fell 9% over the week.

Other major chipmakers also recorded steep losses on Friday.

Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) dropped more than 11%, while Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU) declined over 13%.

The declines reflected broader concerns about valuations and supply chains across the semiconductor industry.

data.title: Evening digest: Anthropic slides after record debut, Bitcoin slips below $60k
data.description:
US markets remained under pressure on Friday as Anthropic shares fell over 10% in their second trading session, adding to concerns about the artificial intelligence trade.

Bitcoin dropped below $60,000 for the first time since July as record outflows from BlackRock's spot ETF and broader risk aversion weighed on cryptocurrencies.

Gold prices slid to a 14-month low and headed for their steepest weekly decline in eight months amid expectations of further Federal Reserve rate increases.

Oil prices also fell, with Brent crude on track for a third consecutive weekly decline as strong Middle Eastern exports outweighed concerns about disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.

Anthropic stock falls nearly 10% on second trading day

Anthropic shares extended their decline on Friday after failing to sustain the gains from their blockbuster Nasdaq debut.

The stock fell 10.52% to trade at $86.95. The stock remained slightly above its IPO price of $83.

The decline followed a volatile debut on Thursday, when Anthropic opened at $111.50, reached a high of $115.10 and closed at $97.17.

More than 846 million shares changed hands during the first session.

The weakness reflects broader concerns about AI-related investments rather than company-specific developments alone.

Investors had hoped Anthropic's record listing would restore confidence in AI stocks, which have faced pressure over the scale and profitability of data centre and chip spending.

Anthropic's underwriters exercised their option to purchase all 147 million additional shares, bringing the total offering to $93.5 billion.

The stock remained above its IPO price, but its early gains had narrowed considerably.

Bitcoin price falls below $60,000

Bitcoin dropped below $60,000 on Friday for the first time since early July, extending a broad cryptocurrency selloff.

The largest cryptocurrency traded at $58,261, down 7.1% over 24 hours. It is now approximately 53% below its record high of $126,296 reached on October 6, 2025.

Selling pressure also affected other major cryptocurrencies.

Ether fell below $1,700 for the first time since July 3, trading at $1,604, while XRP and Solana declined 5% and 5.5%, respectively.

Outflows from US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds added to the pressure.

BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust recorded $541.1 million in net outflows on November 19, its largest single-day withdrawal on record, according to Farside Investors.

US spot Bitcoin ETFs collectively lost $582.3 million that day and approximately $3.47 billion so far in November.

More than $700 million in cryptocurrency positions were liquidated over 24 hours, mostly bullish bets, according to CoinGlass.

Gold price hits 14-month low

Gold extended its decline on Friday, with spot prices falling 2.69% to $3,524.29 an ounce after touching $3,513.54, the lowest level since September 2025.

Bullion was down approximately 9.2% for the week, its steepest weekly decline since March.

US gold futures for December delivery fell 4.2% to $3,530.40 an ounce.

A stronger dollar and expectations of higher US interest rates have weighed on the precious metal.

Markets were pricing in a 96% probability of a 25-basis-point rate increase in December, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

The selloff in AI-linked equities may also have prompted investors to liquidate gold positions to cover losses elsewhere in their portfolios.

Silver fell 3.6% to $41.23 an ounce, while platinum and palladium declined 2.6% and 2.1%, respectively. All four precious metals were heading for a second consecutive weekly decline.

Oil prices head for third weekly decline

Oil prices were mixed on Friday but remained on track for a third consecutive weekly decline as strong exports from the Middle East helped ease supply concerns.

Brent crude futures gained 0.22% to $92.17 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate December futures rose 0.83% to $83.90.

Brent was heading for a weekly loss of nearly 5%, while December WTI was set to fall 5.8%.

Crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have returned to roughly pre-war levels, strengthening expectations of a potential supply surplus.

However, geopolitical risks remain.

The Iran-aligned Houthi movement threatened Saudi Arabia's Red Sea ports after launching missile attacks on Riyadh.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy also said two oil tankers had struck naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz and were burning.

The market is also monitoring OPEC+ discussions scheduled for November 29, when ministers will consider the group's 2027 output policy.
